property_summary: For every state of the contract, paused() returns the value of the internal _paused flag; the mutant returns the negation and thus for some inputs (when _paused is true or false) paused() will differ.

For every call, C.paused() returns the internal _paused flag (i.e. paused() == false immediately after initialize and == true after pause()); the mutant negates this so for some fuzzed inputs the observed paused() value differs (specifically after calling pause/unpause sequences).

For every sequence of pause/unpause calls driven by an admin/manager role, the reference contract's paused() returns the actual internal _paused flag (i.e., paused() reflects whether the contract is paused); the mutant returns the negation and therefore for some fuzzed sequences of calls and actor roles the observed paused() value will differ.

For any sequence of calls, the public paused() getter of the reference contract returns the internal paused state (_paused) while the mutant returns its negation, so there exists sequences (e.g., after calling pause or unpause) where paused() differs between reference and mutant.

Invariant: the public paused() getter returns the actual internal pause state of the contract (i.e., paused() == false before pause() and == true after pause()); the mutant negates the internal flag so paused() will differ for some inputs (specifically after calling pause()), causing the property to fail.

For every call, paused() returns the contract's internal paused state (_paused) — the reference returns the actual _paused flag while the mutant always returns true, breaking the property for inputs where _paused is false.

For every call, the contract's paused() getter returns the actual paused state (true iff _pause() was called and not _unpause()); the mutant always returns false, so there exist inputs where paused() != true while contract is actually paused.

For every sequence of calls, the reference's paused() reflects the contract pause state (true after pause() until unpause()), whereas the mutant always returns false, so there exist inputs where paused() is true on the reference but false on the mutant.

For any caller address, calling pause() by an address with MANAGER role makes c.paused() return true (contract reports paused) until unpause(); the mutant that hardcodes paused() to false violates this because after pause() it still returns false for some caller addresses.

For every address input, calling paused() on the correct contract returns the actual paused state (it can be true after pause() by a manager), whereas the mutant that forces paused() to always return false will produce a different returned boolean for some inputs (when the contract is paused) — so the property: paused() == (contract actually paused) holds for all inputs on reference but is violated by the mutant.

For every caller address that is an LRT manager, invoking pause() makes the reference contract report paused() == true (until unpause), whereas the mutant that forces paused() to always return false will return false after pause() for some manager caller — so the property is: if pause() succeeds then paused() == true.

For any nonzero address input, calling updateLRTConfig(addr) succeeds (does not revert) and sets lrtConfig to that address; the mutant that removes the non-zero check additionally allows the zero address, so the reference enforces that zero address cannot be set whereas the mutant permits it (causing lrtConfig==address(0)).

For all addresses a, calling updateLRTConfig(a) on the correct contract either reverts when a == address(0) or results in lrtConfig() != address(0); the mutant that removed the non-zero check allows successfully setting lrtConfig to address(0), violating this rule.

For every address input, calling updateLRTConfig(addr) on the correct contract either reverts when addr == address(0) (preventing lrtConfig from becoming zero) or results in lrtConfig() != address(0); the mutant that removed the non-zero check allows setting lrtConfig to address(0), violating this invariant for some input (addr == address(0)).

For any address input, calling updateLRTConfig(addr) on the correct contract never leaves lrtConfig as the zero address (the call reverts for addr==address(0)); the mutant that removed the non-zero check can set lrtConfig to address(0), violating this invariant for the input addr == address(0).

For all addresses passed to updateLRTConfig by an account with the admin role, the reference contract refuses (reverts) when given the zero address (so lrtConfig never becomes address(0)), while the mutant accepts zero and sets lrtConfig to address(0); the property: after calling updateLRTConfig as the admin, c.lrtConfig() != address(0) for every input — the mutant violates this for input address(0).

For any caller address, the reference contract allows only an account holding the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE in lrtConfig to successfully call updateLRTConfig (i.e. only such callers make updateLRTConfig return/complete), whereas the mutant incorrectly allows callers holding the MANAGER role to succeed instead, so there exist caller addresses for which the reference rejects updateLRTConfig but the mutant accepts it.

For any lrtConfig contract and any caller, only callers that have the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE according to lrtConfig are allowed to successfully call C.updateLRTConfig(...); the mutant instead permits callers with the MANAGER role to succeed, so there exist callers for which the reference reverts but the mutant returns successfully.

For any caller and any lrtConfigAddr, the reference C only allows updateLRTConfig to succeed when lrtConfig.hasRole(DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE, caller) is true; the mutant incorrectly allows callers with the MANAGER role to call updateLRTConfig, so there exist inputs (a caller having MANAGER but not DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE) where reference reverts but mutant succeeds.

For any provided lrtConfigAddr and caller, the correct contract only allows updateLRTConfig to succeed when the caller holds the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE in lrtConfig; the mutant instead allows callers holding the MANAGER role — so there exist lrtConfig implementations and caller addresses where the reference reverts but the mutant returns successfully.

For any lrtConfig contract address and any caller, C.updateLRTConfig(lrtConfigAddr) only succeeds (does not revert) when the caller is granted the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE by that lrtConfig; the mutant incorrectly allows callers with the MANAGER role to succeed, so there exist lrtConfig implementations and caller addresses where the reference reverts but the mutant returns successfully.

After initialize(...) completes, maxNodeDelegatorCount equals the configured default (10) for the correct contract for every input, whereas the mutant sets it to 0 causing a mismatch for some inputs; the test checks that initialize results in maxNodeDelegatorCount == 10.

For any nonzero lrtConfig address passed to initialize, the reference contract always sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to a positive nonzero default (10) after initialization, whereas the mutant sets it to 0 for some input; we assert that after initialize returns successfully the public getter maxNodeDelegatorCount() is nonzero.

For any nonzero lrtConfig address that allows initialize to succeed, after calling initialize(...) the reference contract leaves maxNodeDelegatorCount strictly greater than the length of nodeDelegatorQueue (since reference initializes maxNodeDelegatorCount to 10 and queue starts empty), whereas the mutant can set maxNodeDelegatorCount to 0 causing maxNodeDelegatorCount() <= nodeDelegatorQueue().length for some inputs.

For every nonzero lrtConfig address that allows initialize to succeed, after initialize(...) returns successfully the reference sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to a positive value (>0), whereas the mutant may set it to 0, so the universal rule is: if initialize succeeds then c.maxNodeDelegatorCount() > 0; the mutant violates this for some admissible input.

For any non-zero lrtConfig address, a successful call to initialize(...) must result in maxNodeDelegatorCount equal to 10 in the reference implementation, while the mutant sets it to 0 and thus violates that invariant for some inputs.

After initialize(...) completes, maxNodeDelegatorCount equals 10 for the correct contract for every input; the mutant that increments it makes maxNodeDelegatorCount != 10 for some inputs (specifically any initialize call), so the property is that c.maxNodeDelegatorCount() == 10 after initialize is always true for the reference and broken by the mutant.

After calling initialize(lrtConfigAddr) with any non-zero lrtConfigAddr the correct contract always sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to an INITIAL value that is exactly 10, whereas the mutant increments it to 11 and thus violates this invariant for those inputs.

For any non-zero lrtConfig address, after calling initialize(lrtConfigAddr) the reference contract sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to exactly 10; the mutant increments it to 11 and thus violates this equality for some input lrtConfigAddr.

For every non-zero lrtConfig address, calling initialize(lrtConfigAddr) on the correct contract leaves maxNodeDelegatorCount equal to 10 (the intended initial cap); the mutant increments it after assignment making the stored value 11 for those same calls, so asserting the stored value equals 10 distinguishes them.

For any non-zero lrtConfigAddr, calling initialize(lrtConfigAddr) on the correct contract leaves maxNodeDelegatorCount equal to the single-assignment value 10 (no further increments); the mutant that adds an extra increment makes maxNodeDelegatorCount > 10 for some admissible inputs, so the property is that after initialize the stored maxNodeDelegatorCount equals 10.

For any nonzero lrtConfig address, after initialize(...) completes the reference contract sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to 10, whereas the mutant leaves it at 0 (so maxNodeDelegatorCount == 10 always holds for the reference but is false for some inputs for the mutant).

After initialize(...) with any non-zero lrtConfig address, the reference contract sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to 10; the mutant omits that assignment leaving it 0, so the property maxNodeDelegatorCount() == 10 holds for all admissible inputs in the reference but is violated by the mutant for some input.

After calling initialize with any non-zero lrtConfig address, the reference contract always sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to 10; the mutant omits that assignment leaving it 0, so the property maxNodeDelegatorCount() == 10 for every admissible input is violated by the mutant for some input.

For any non-zero lrtConfig address passed to initialize, the reference contract sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to 10 (so c.maxNodeDelegatorCount() == 10); the mutant omits this assignment leaving it 0, thus violating the property for inputs where the provided lrtConfig address is non-zero.

For any non-zero lrtConfig address passed to initialize, the reference contract sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to 10 (so c.maxNodeDelegatorCount() == 10); the mutant omits that assignment leaving it 0, thus violating this invariant for at least some input lrtConfig addresses.

After calling initialize(lrtConfigAddr) from any caller with any nonzero lrtConfigAddr, the reference contract always sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to 10; the mutant that sets _initialized = 2 in the initializer can cause initialize's body to be skipped in some deployment/upgrade patterns and thus may leave maxNodeDelegatorCount != 10 for some inputs.
